Solvatochromic Parameters of Deep Eutectic Solvents: Effect of Different Carboxylic Acids as Hydrogen Bond Donor Amos K. Dwamena and Douglas E. Raynie*
Cite This: J. Chem. Eng. Data 2020, 65, 640–646 Read Online

ACCESS | Metrics & More | Article Recommendations | Supporting Information ABSTRACT: The physicochemical properties of carboxylic acid-based deep eutectic solvents (DESs) were measured by solvatochromic probes: Nile red, N,N-diethyl-4-nitroaniline, and 4-nitroaniline. UV-vis absorbance of these probes was computed with temperature in the range of 298.15 to 318.15 K. By increasing temperature, the normalized polarity of DESs stayed linear except for [Ch]Cl:butyric acid (1:3) and [Ch]Cl:caprylic acid (1:2), which had a modest shift in the maximum wavelength between T = (308.15 to 318.15) K. Changes in the normalized polarity parameter of DESs demonstrated an interesting trend, and it confirms that alkyl chain length of the hydrogen bond donor (HBD) affects the solvation microsphere of the solute-solvent interaction. Also, dipolarity/polarizability (π*) and hydrogen bond acidity (a) decrease with increasing alkyl chain length confirming the significant contribution of HBDs to Kamlet-Taft parameters. Interestingly, the π* and a parameters of DESs did not change significantly and seem to be independent of temperature. <::transcription of the content : figure::> In addition, density functional theory was used to extend our understanding on how alkyl chain length of HBD affects charge transfer in the DESs. In summary, both solvatochromic molecular probes and density functional theory are effective methods for studying polarity parameters and charge transfer, respectively, for DESs with varying alkyl chain length of the hydrogen bond donor.

## 1. INTRODUCTION Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) are a new generation of designer solvents alternative to ionic liquids.1,2 The term was first introduced by Abbott and his co-workers by mixing choline chloride and urea at 1:2 molar ratio, with a depressed melting point compared to the individual components.1,2 Simply put, the formation of DESs involves the combination of a salt acting as a hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) with a hydrogen bond donor (HBD) in the correct molar ratio until the eutectic point is reached. The driving force for the eutectic point is hydrogen bonding interaction between the chloride anion of the salt and the proton of the HBD, resulting in charge delocalization.2,3 Since its first inception, many independent researchers have worked with different HBA and HBD to understand the nature, physicochemical behavior, and thermophysical properties of the solvent.4-7 Choline chloride, [Ch]Cl, remains the most used salt for DES formation due to its low cost, low toxicity, biodegradability, and biocompatibility whereas some commonly used HBDs include urea, alcohol, sugar, amide, amino acid, and carboxylic acid.7,8

Carboxylic acid-based DESs have recently attracted attention due to their uniqueness in analytical extraction, 9,10 organic synthesis, 6 electrochemistry, and pharmaceutics. 12 Commonly used monocarboxylic acids, dicarboxylic acids, and tricarboxylic acids in DES formulation include acetic acid, oxalic acid, malonic acid, malic acid, maleic acid, levulinic acid, and citric acid. 13,14 Recently, a hydrophobic DES was
synthesized from decanoic acid and quaternary ammonium salts and the solvent was found to have higher extraction efficiency for volatile organic compounds (VOCs). 15

Despite the numerous physicochemical and thermochemical data on carboxylic acid-based DESs, little or no attempt has been made to understand the molecular interactions that occur within these solvent systems. For example, a pioneering work by Abbott et al.1,2 inferred that two carboxylic acids might be required to complex each chloride anion for the eutectic point to be reached. Over a decade of this postulation, a detailed molecular explanation on how this complexation occurs is still missing in the literature. Recently, the solvatochromic properties and molecular dynamic simulations were performed on DESs formulated from choline chloride and urea, ethaline, and glycerol to show hydrogen bonding.16

In this work, DESs with different molar ratios of choline chloride and butyric acid (BA), valeric acid (VA), and caprylic acid (CA) were studied by using solvatochromic probes and density functional theory (DFT). For DFT, the frontier molecular orbitals (FMOs), which are known to contain useful information for chemical reactions, were used to study charge transfer of DES mixtures. 17-20 Moreover, these hydrogen bond

To date, most DESs have been hydrophilic,²¹ hence studying the solvatochromic and charge transfer properties of these hydrophobic DESs would be the first of its kind. The longest wavelength intermolecular charge transfer polarity scale by Kosower²² was normalized by Nile red (NR) dye to determine the electron transition (E_T or Z) (eq 1).²³ The Kamlet–Taft (KT) multiparameter linear polarity parameters (hydrogen bonding acidity, α; hydrogen bonding basicity, β; dipolarity/polar- izability, π*) were determined using 4-nitroaniline (4NA) and N,N-diethyl-4-nitroaniline (DENA) as the molecular solvato- chromic probes (eqs 2–4).

To fully understand how hydrogen bond donors alter charge transfer, dipole moments, and other thermophysical properties of DESs, a density functional theory (DFT) employing Beck's three-parameter exchange functional²⁴ and Lee–Yang–Parr correlation functional²⁵ (B3LYP) at the 6-312 (d) basis set was used to study the FMOs. In this study, experimental procedures by using solvatochromic molecular probes and DFT were explored to help understand how hydrogen bond donors and hydrogen bond acceptors behave during DES formulation.

## 2.2. Synthesis of DESs. DESs were synthesized by following the procedure described¹⁴ with some modifications. This involves mixing choline chloride and butyric acid, valeric acid, and caprylic acid at 1:2 and 1:3 molar ratios. The mixture was heated at 80 °C for 15–30 min under constant stirring at an atmospheric pressure until a homogenous liquid was obtained. The prepared DESs were cooled to room temperature and stored in a desiccator before use.

## 2.3. Solvatochromism. A UV–vis spectrophotometer (Synergy H1 microplate reader, Biotek) was used to determine the maximum absorption wavelength ($\lambda_{max}$) of DESs in solvatochromic probes. Absorbance readings were collected by spectral scanning of DESs in Nile red at $\lambda$ = (400 to 650) nm, N,N-diethyl-4-nitroaniline at $\lambda$ = (300 to 450) nm, and 4-nitroaniline at $\lambda$ = (300 to 450) nm at 1 nm interval in triplicate. The working concentration for all the solvatochromic probes was kept as low as 0.5 × 10$^{-4}$ M to help neglect the effect of solute–solute interaction.$^{26}$ The effect of temperature on electron transition in the probes and on the Kamlet–Taft parameters was obtained at T = (298.15 to 318.15) K. The unit of electron transition in Nile red, E$_T$ (NR), is in kcal. mol$^{-1}$, $\nu$ is the wavenumber, and $\lambda_{max}$ is the maximum wavelength in nanometer (nm). ## 2.4. Computational Method. Quantum theoretical calculations were performed with the Gaussian 09 software package integrated with the Gauss View 5.0.8 graphical interface.30 Gas-phase equilibrium geometries were fully optimized with vibrational frequencies calculated using DFT/B3LYP at the 6-31G (d) basis set. The DFT/B3LYP functional makes correction for both gradient and exchange correlations and provides qualitative results, which have comparable accuracy compared to ab initio methods at a reduced CPU time. The absence of imaginary frequency showed that structures are at true minima.31 The molecular orbital calculations for optimized HBA, HBD, and DESs were executed with the same computational method and basis sets at 298 K to obtain the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) energies. The HOMO–LUMO gap and charge transfer (ΔN) of DESs were calculated.

## 3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION ### 3.1. Physical Characterization of DESs. Several carboxylic acid-based DESs have been reported in the literature, but data on the electronic properties of these solvents are sporadic. Also, little or no work has been done to elucidate how an increased hydrocarbon chain length of fatty acids affects solvatochromic parameters and charge transfer of DESs. In this work, three hydrogen bond donors (HBDs) were selected to tailor the physicochemical behavior of DESs by increasing their alkyl chain length. Butyric acid (BA), valeric acid (VA), and caprylic acid (CA) are cheap, readily available, biodegradable, and nontoxic making them excellent HBDs for this research. In Table 2, choline chloride with either butyric acid or valeric acid at 1:3 molar ratio forms a transparent liquid at room temperature, whereas choline chloride with caprylic acid at the same molar ratio appears cloudy. The high viscosities of [Ch]Cl:BA, [Ch]Cl:VA, and [Ch]Cl:CA DESs (1:2) are partly due to hydrogen bonding and charge transfer occurring between the cation and the chloride anion (Table S1). DESs at 1:1 molar ratio stay solid at room temperature.

## 3.2. Solvatochromism. 3.2.1. Electron Transition (E_T) between Solvent and Solute. Solvatochromism, due to its simplicity, remains the most widely used method for studying empirical solvent polarity because the spectrum of the probes (solute) changes when it dissolves in different solvent molecules in the microsphere solvation of probes. The use of a 96-well microplate UV–vis spectrophotometer equipped with a 4-Zone™ incubator made it easier to control temperature between _T_ = (298 and 318) K. Nile red, instead of penta-_tert_-butyl-substituted betaine dye by Dimroth and Reichardt, was used to calculate _E_T values due to the highly acidic character of the DESs. The π* measures the nonspecific interactions such as dipole–dipole and dipole-induced dipole interactions and the polarizability occurring between the dye and the DESs. From the results, nonspecific interactions serve as an index for DES polarity and it decreases with increasing hydrocarbon chain length of the HBD. 3.3.2. HOMO and LUMO Energies. The highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) were calculated for DESs including their corresponding constituents. These orbitals are important in quantum chemistry because electrons are mostly located in them for reactions. The HOMO defines a region where

electrons have the highest energy for reaction, whereas the LUMO creates a region for invading electrons from other molecules to fill-in during bonding. In other terms, the HOMO donates electrons (ionization potential) into the LUMO, which tend to act as the orbital's electron affinity (ability to obtain electrons). From the results (Table S2), the ionization potential of the HBD decreases as the alkyl increases. As expected, the ionization potential of the HBD is greater than the HBA and the electron affinity of the HBA is greater than the HBD. Among the hydrogen bond donors, those with two molar ratios have the highest ionization potential (Table S2).

The difference in energy between these frontier molecular orbitals (HOMO–LUMO gap) is critical to study molecular reactivity, global hardness, electronegativity, chemical potential, and charge transfer within the molecule. The higher the HOMO–LUMO gap, the less reactive the molecule because electrons have wider distance to jump and the molecule becomes more stable. Among the raw materials studied, choline chloride has the smallest electronic gap of 0.18477 eV, which makes it most reactive and least stable compared to all the HBD with electronic gaps between 0.2688 and 0.28527 eV. The global hardness (wider HOMO–LUMO gap) of the DESs increased marginally when the molar ratio of the HBD changed but no apparent change occurred by increasing the alkyl chain length. The hardness and softness (shorter HOMO–LUMO gap) property of DESs is important especially when the solvent is applied in chemical reactions, organic synthesis, pharmaceuticals, and electrochemistry. The clear understanding of this phenomenon is essential to help choose the correct solvent for desired industrial and pharmaceutical purposes.

3.3.3. Charge Transfer (ΔN). As stated by Sanderson in the electronegativity equalization principle, 36,37 the combination of HBA and HBD leads to electron flow from the species of lower electronegativity to species of higher electronegativity until the adduct (in this case, DESs) electronegativity becomes equalized. The electronegativity of the HBA, HBD, and DESs were calculated from the FMOs using Mulliken's formulae 37,38 [χ = (I + A)/2]. From the results (Table S2), electrons flow from the HBA (χ = 0.079475) to the HBD (0.131845 ≤ χ ≤ 0.13823). The electronegativity values of the DESs are closer to the geometric mean of the starting raw materials. The chemical potential (Lagrange multiplier, μ = −χ), a new density functional parameter by Parr et al., 17,37 was calculated as an index to measure charge transfer between the HBA and the HBD in the formulated DESs. The electronegativity and chemical potential of DESs are similar when the same molar ratio of HBD is used irrespective of the alkyl chain length (Table S3). As shown in Figure 6, the electron flow pattern indicates that the HOMO structure of [Ch]Cl:BA (1:2) has electron density localized on the chloride anion (light green) while the LUMO electron cloud is localized on the nitrogen (blue) and hydrogen (white) of the HBA. As displayed in Table 4, the HOMO and LUMO data obtained by the DFT calculations were used to calculate charge transfer occurring within the solvent. Also, the calculated electronic gap is a measure of the DES stability.

As shown in Table 5, it is not surprising that the [Ch]Cl:BA (1:2) DES has the highest charge transfer of 0.250806 followed by 0.248927 of [Ch]Cl:VA (1:2) and 0.246531 of [Ch]Cl:CA (1:2). INTRODUCTION Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) are a new generation of designer solvents alternative to ionic liquids.1,2 The term was first introduced by Abbott and his co-workers by mixing choline chloride and urea at 1:2 molar ratio, with a depressed melting point compared to the individual components.1,2 Simply put, the formation of DESs involves the combination of a salt acting as a hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) with a hydrogen bond donor (HBD) in the correct molar ratio until the eutectic point is reached. The driving force for the eutectic point is hydrogen bonding interaction between the chloride anion of the salt and the proton of the HBD, resulting in charge delocalization.2,3 Since its first inception, many independent researchers have worked with different HBA and HBD to understand the nature, physicochemical behavior, and thermophysical properties of the solvent.4-7 Choline chloride, [Ch]Cl, remains the most used salt for DES formation due to its low cost, low toxicity, biodegradability, and biocompatibility whereas some commonly used HBDs include urea, alcohol, sugar, amide, amino acid, and carboxylic acid.7,8 Carboxylic acid-based DESs have recently attracted attention due to their uniqueness in analytical extraction, 9,10 organic synthesis, 6 electrochemistry, and pharmaceutics. 12 Commonly used monocarboxylic acids, dicarboxylic acids, and tricarboxylic acids in DES formulation include acetic acid, oxalic acid, malonic acid, malic acid, maleic acid, levulinic acid, and citric acid. 13,14 Recently, a hydrophobic DES was synthesized from decanoic acid and quaternary ammonium salts and the solvent was found to have higher extraction efficiency for volatile organic compounds (VOCs). 15 Despite the numerous physicochemical and thermochemical data on carboxylic acid-based DESs, little or no attempt has been made to understand the molecular interactions that occur within these solvent systems. For example, a pioneering work by Abbott et al.1,2 inferred that two carboxylic acids might be required to complex each chloride anion for the eutectic point to be reached. Over a decade of this postulation, a detailed molecular explanation on how this complexation occurs is still missing in the literature. Recently, the solvatochromic properties and molecular dynamic simulations were performed on DESs formulated from choline chloride and urea, ethaline, and glycerol to show hydrogen bonding.16 In this work, DESs with different molar ratios of choline chloride and butyric acid (BA), valeric acid (VA), and caprylic acid (CA) were studied by using solvatochromic probes and density functional theory (DFT). The highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) were calculated for DESs including their corresponding constituents. These orbitals are important in quantum chemistry because electrons are mostly located in them for reactions. The HOMO defines a region where electrons have the highest energy for reaction, whereas the LUMO creates a region for invading electrons from other molecules to fill-in during bonding. In other terms, the HOMO donates electrons (ionization potential) into the LUMO, which tend to act as the orbital's electron affinity (ability to obtain electrons). From the results (Table S2), the ionization potential of the HBD decreases as the alkyl increases. As expected, the ionization potential of the HBD is greater than the HBA and the electron affinity of the HBA is greater than the HBD. Among the hydrogen bond donors, those with two molar ratios have the highest ionization potential (Table S2). The difference in energy between these frontier molecular orbitals (HOMO–LUMO gap) is critical to study molecular reactivity, global hardness, electronegativity, chemical potential, and charge transfer within the molecule. The higher the HOMO–LUMO gap, the less reactive the molecule because electrons have wider distance to jump and the molecule becomes more stable. Among the raw materials studied, choline chloride has the smallest electronic gap of 0.18477 eV, which makes it most reactive and least stable compared to all the HBD with electronic gaps between 0.2688 and 0.28527 eV. The global hardness (wider HOMO–LUMO gap) of the DESs increased marginally when the molar ratio of the HBD changed but no apparent change occurred by increasing the alkyl chain length. The hardness and softness (shorter HOMO–LUMO gap) property of DESs is important especially when the solvent is applied in chemical reactions, organic synthesis, pharmaceuticals, and electrochemistry. The clear understanding of this phenomenon is essential to help choose the correct solvent for desired industrial and pharmaceutical purposes. 3.3.3. Charge Transfer (ΔN). As stated by Sanderson in the electronegativity equalization principle, 36,37 the combination of HBA and HBD leads to electron flow from the species of lower electronegativity to species of higher electronegativity until the adduct (in this case, DESs) electronegativity becomes equalized. CONCLUSIONS A modest attempt to study physicochemical and thermophysical properties of carboxylic acid-based DESs by using solvatochromic probes and density functional theory was studied. A bathochromic shift was observed when [Ch]Cl:BA (1:3) DES interacts with a Nile red solvatochromic probe. An increase in the alkyl chain length of the hydrogen bond donor decreases the polarity of the DESs. Moreover, the electronic transition of DESs in Nile red is a single parameter, which can be used to estimate the polarity of the formulated solvent. Also, the Kamlet-Taft hydrogen bonding acidity (α), hydrogen bonding basicity (β), and polarizability/dipolarity (π*) of the newly formed DESs were comparable to selected ionic liquids and organic solvents in the literature. In addition, density functional theory expanded our understanding that DESs at 1:2 molar ratio have high charge transfer and dipole moments occurring within the solvent. The DFT results confirm earlier assertions that two carboxylic acids are required for some DES formation. **ASSOCIATED CONTENT** **S** Supporting Information The Supporting Information is available free of charge at https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.jced.9b00872. CONCLUSIONS A modest attempt to study physicochemical and thermophysical properties of carboxylic acid-based DESs by using solvatochromic probes and density functional theory was studied. A bathochromic shift was observed when [Ch]Cl:BA (1:3) DES interacts with a Nile red solvatochromic probe. An increase in the alkyl chain length of the hydrogen bond donor decreases the polarity of the DESs. Moreover, the electronic transition of DESs in Nile red is a single parameter, which can be used to estimate the polarity of the formulated solvent. Also, the Kamlet-Taft hydrogen bonding acidity (α), hydrogen bonding basicity (β), and polarizability/dipolarity (π*) of the newly formed DESs were comparable to selected ionic liquids and organic solvents in the literature. In addition, density functional theory expanded our understanding that DESs at 1:2 molar ratio have high charge transfer and dipole moments occurring within the solvent.
